newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Thousands in Belgrade streets, police carry rifles.
newsitem.headline: Thousands in Belgrade streets, police carry rifles.

text.p: Tens of thousands of demonstrators thronged central Belgrade on Wednesday, keeping up pressure on Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic to deliver on a promise to reinstate opposition election victories.

Iron-grey ranks of paramilitary police were out in strength too. This time they did not leave their automatic rifles behind in their buses as usual but carried them slung over their shoulders, witnesses said.
Teargas guns and CS gas cartridges were also within reach.
The autocratic Milosevic suddenly announced on Tuesday, the 77th day of relentless protests, that he was asking parliament to reinstate disputed results of November's local elections.

Two days earlier he had ordered his anti-riot police to forcibly break up the Belgrade demonstrations. Repeated baton charges left scores injured in the worst street violence seen in Belgrade for years and prompted an international outcry.
Diplomats said Milosevic's decision was not unexpected, but they wondered why it took three months.
Authoritative political sources in Serbia told Reuters it took time for moderates to overcome diehard opinion within Milosevic's socialist establishment.
Leaders of Serbia's three-party opposition coalition, while giving a cautious welcome to the apparent climbdown, have nevertheless insisted on continuing the protests.
There were many sceptics among Wednesday's 50,000-strong crowds packing the tree-lined avenues and cobbled pedestrian precincts of central Belgrade.

"I do not trust them at all -- even when I buy (the pro-government newspaper) Politika, I check the date to see if it's correct," opposition politician Vuk Draskovic told the marchers, who whistled, stamped, cheered and blew horns.
"We will sooner have babies before they recognise anything," said economist Zarko Sakic, 40.
"I was beaten six times and if need be let them beat me 20 times more because this is my way to protest against this lying regime," said a shabbily dressed man in his 30s.

An engineer in suit and tie shrugged. "All of what we do is completely ridiculous but I will miss the demonstrations when they end...people found a lot of wit in them, high spirits, new friends and new loves," he said.
The scepticsm was shared by foreign governments.
French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said he hoped Milosevic's decision was not simply a delaying tactic.
Washington has said it welcomed the move "as a first step in the right direction in Serbia".

Milosevic's move to have parliament, dominated by his Socialist Party, enact a special bill to uphold the November election outcome in keeping with recommendations of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), seemed clear cut at first.
But some experts questioned whether the solution was constitutional.
Constitutional court judge Slobodan Vucetic said Milosevic was empowered only to urge courts to establish the truth about the election results, not have parliament decide the matter.

Drago Hiber, legal committee chief of the Zajedno (Together opposition coalition), said he expected further wrangling over the findings of the OSCE mission and "what this special law should recognise".

The 54-nation OSCE, from which Yugoslavia has been suspended, verified that Zajedno won the municipal vote in 14 towns and cities, including Belgrade, without "irregularities" cited by the ruling Socialists when they nullified the results.
But the opposition also demands an independent judiciary and free media ahead of parliamentary and presidential elections due by the end of this year.

Opposition leaders were quick to note that police deployed in Belgrade were more heavily armed that usual. As well as their pistols, shields, one-metre(yard)-long batons, they carried the M-72, the Yugoslav-made Kalashnikov rifle.
"Emotions are often quicker than reason -- many people have been beaten -- but please, please, clench your teeth and understand every blow you get is also a medal," said Draskovic.
"Do not give them any motive to beat us -- go home after the protest," he told the crowd.
